title: Crypto 101: What Cryptocurrencies Are Used For, From Payments to DeFi
summary: A plain-English tour of what people actually do with crypto, from payments and trading to lending, staking and yield farming, and the risks that come with each.
body:
Cryptocurrency started as a way to send money without a bank in the middle. It has grown into a set of tools that can do much of what traditional finance does, and some things it cannot. Each of those uses carries its own risks, and some carry legal consequences people do not expect.

This article is general information, not legal, tax or investment advice.

## The basics

A cryptocurrency is a digital asset recorded on a blockchain, a shared ledger kept by many computers. You hold it in a wallet controlled by a private key. Bitcoin was the first, launched in 2009. Ethereum and similar networks added smart contracts, programs that run on the blockchain and make most of the activities below possible.

## Payments and stablecoins

The simplest use is sending value. Crypto transfers can settle quickly, any day of the week, across borders. Because most cryptocurrencies swing in price, many payments now use stablecoins, tokens designed to hold a steady value, usually one U.S. dollar. A federal law passed in 2025 created the first national rules for issuers of payment stablecoins.

## Trading

Many people buy crypto hoping it will rise in value. Centralized exchanges hold your assets for you, much like a brokerage. Decentralized exchanges use smart contracts to trade directly from your own wallet. That keeps you in control, but if something goes wrong there is usually no customer service to call.

## Leverage

Some platforms let traders borrow to make bigger bets. With leverage, a small price move can produce a large gain or wipe out the position entirely, and positions are often closed automatically, or liquidated, when the price moves against the trader. U.S. law also limits which leveraged and derivative products can be offered to people in the United States, and many offshore platforms are not permitted to serve U.S. customers.

## Hedging

The same tools can reduce risk. A holder might hedge by moving part of a position into stablecoins, or by using futures or options to offset losses if prices fall. Hedging can limit the downside, but it costs money and does not remove risk completely.

## Decentralized finance: lending and borrowing

Decentralized finance, or DeFi, means financial services run by smart contracts instead of banks.

- Lending: you deposit crypto into a lending pool and earn interest paid by borrowers.
- Borrowing: you lock up crypto as collateral, usually worth more than the loan, and borrow against it. If the collateral falls in value, the protocol can sell it automatically to repay the loan.

People borrow against crypto to get cash without selling, but a sharp price drop can mean losing the collateral quickly.

## Staking

Many blockchains are secured by participants who lock up, or stake, their coins and help validate transactions, earning rewards in return. You can stake directly, through a pooled service or through an exchange. Staked coins may be locked for a period, and some networks take away part of a stake if a validator misbehaves.

## Yield farming and liquidity pools

Decentralized exchanges need pools of tokens to trade against. Users who deposit pairs of tokens into those pools earn a share of the trading fees, and sometimes extra reward tokens. Moving funds between protocols to chase the highest return is often called yield farming. Advertised returns can be high, but so are the risks: price swings between the paired tokens, reward tokens that lose value, and code that can be exploited.

## Risks across the board

- Volatility: prices can move sharply in hours.
- Smart contract risk: bugs and exploits have drained protocols of large sums.
- Counterparty risk: exchanges and lenders can fail and freeze customer funds.
- Scams: fake platforms, impersonators and promises of sure returns are common.
- Irreversibility: transfers generally cannot be undone.

## Where the law comes in

- Taxes: the IRS treats digital assets as property. Selling, swapping or spending crypto can create a taxable gain or loss, and staking and lending rewards are generally treated as income when you receive them. Brokers now report many crypto sales to the IRS.
- Securities: some tokens, and some lending or yield programs, have been treated as securities offerings, which brings registration requirements and investor protections into play.
- Records: keep track of what you bought, when, what you paid and what you received.
- Estate planning: if no one can reach your keys, your family may not be able to reach your assets.

The rules are changing quickly at both the federal and state level, so check for current information before you act.
